children: used its Ignite conference to show how it plans to make money from AI beyond Copilot subscriptions. The company announced new tools for automating office work, offered select customers access to its AI model weights, and outlined how its own chips could make Azure more efficient as AI usage grows.
In Microsoft 365, the new Copilot Workspaces gives employees and AI agents a shared place to manage projects. An agent called Autopilot can handle recurring tasks without a prompt at every step.
Microsoft also previewed a Salesforce integration with more than 38 built-in sales functions, giving teams access to tools they already use from inside Copilot.

On the cloud side, Microsoft made its Cobalt 200 virtual machines generally available and plans to expand them to 23 Azure regions by year-end. The company says its upcoming Maia 300 accelerator will generate 40% more tokens per watt than leading GPU-based systems.
Microsoft is also licensing the underlying parameters of some of its own models to select customers, giving businesses more control over how they adapt and deploy them.

More agents could mean more Azure usage if customers put them to work on recurring tasks. The financial test is whether that extra usage can cover the cost of building and operating more data centers.
Oppenheimer sees room for Microsoft to grow AI adoption while protecting margins, with capacity utilization and depreciation among the figures to watch.

title: Microsoft's Next AI Revenue Test Goes Beyond Copilot
